claims.text: Globalisation is the growing integration of the economies of the world, as trade in goods and services across borders widens, companies spread their production and sales across several countries, and information, finance and people move between countries more freely.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: What globalisation includes: goods and services produced in one country and sold in others; companies with operations in more than one country; information and finance moving worldwide; and people travelling, studying and working across borders.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Kaoko Juice presses marula fruit at Opuwo, sells 12 000 bottles a year in Namibian shops, exports 4 000 bottles to Botswana, and buys its glass bottles from a works in Germany and its labels from a printer in Portugal: one small firm, four countries in one bottle.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A multinational company (MNC) is a firm that produces goods or services in more than one country, through plants, offices or other operations it runs there; a firm that sells abroad from its home base is an exporter, not a multinational. The country of its head office is its home country; each other country where it operates is a host country.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The role MNCs play in globalisation: to a host country they may bring investment, jobs, worker training and production know-how, while some of the profit they earn may be paid back to the home country, and local firms may face stronger competition; to the home country they bring profit returned from abroad and wider markets, though jobs and tax revenue may go abroad where production moves to a host country.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Public limited companies vs state-owned companies, as they meet the MNC: a public limited company sells shares on a stock exchange, a state-owned company belongs to a government, and a multinational company produces in more than one country - three different questions, about ownership traded to the public, about who owns it, and about where it operates. One firm may be any combination of the three; the test that tells them apart is to ask which question the sentence answers.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Haneda Electronics keeps its head office in Nagoya, Japan, and has opened an assembly plant in Oshakati paying 300 workers an average of N$6 500 a month; the plant has trained 60 technicians whose skills then spread to other firms in the town, while the profit it earns, about N$12 million a year, is paid to the head office.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Free trade is international trade without government barriers: no tariffs (taxes on imports), no import quotas (limits on the quantity imported) and no embargoes (bans). The word free refers to the absence of barriers, not to the goods being free of charge - goods traded freely still carry prices.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Free trade vs goods being free: free trade is a border policy - goods cross without taxes, quantity limits or bans, though buyers still pay for them; a free good is a good so abundant relative to wants that taking it costs nothing, like sunshine in the Namib. The test that tells them apart: is the sentence about what happens at the border, or about what the good costs?

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The benefits of free trade land on consumers, who tend to face lower prices and wider choice as imports compete with home goods; on producers, who may buy cheaper inputs from abroad and sell into larger markets; and on the economy as a whole, as resources tend to shift towards what the country produces best. A gain to the buyer or seller in the trade is a private benefit; a gain that lands on others is an external benefit; the whole gain to society, private and external together, is the social benefit.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Benefits to individuals vs the country: a benefit to individuals names a person - a consumer paying less for a good, a worker hired by an expanding exporter - while a benefit to the country names the economy as a whole - resources shifting towards the country's best products, wider choice across its markets. The test: name who the question asks about, and answer at that level.

claims.text: Protection is government action that shelters home producers from import competition. Its methods are the tariff (a tax on imported goods), the import quota (a limit on the quantity that may be imported in a period), the subsidy (a payment to home producers that lowers their costs), and the embargo (a ban on trade with a country or in a product).

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: How the methods differ: a tariff raises the price of an import at the border, so the import tends to lose buyers who mind price, and the government collects the tax as revenue; a quota caps the quantity directly, whatever buyers are willing to pay; a subsidy lowers home producers' costs without touching the import, so home goods may price closer to it, with the cost landing on taxpayers; an embargo stops the trade altogether.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A tariff of N$50 is placed on each imported blanket at Walvis Bay. The border price of an imported blanket rises from N$200 to N$250, since N$200 + N$50 = N$250, and the quantity imported in a year falls from 8 000 blankets to 6 000, so the government collects 6 000 x N$50 = N$300 000 in revenue while home blankets at N$230, now N$20 below the import, lift their output from 3 000 towards 3 800.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The reasons governments give for protection: to shelter an infant industry until it grows big enough to produce at a cost per unit close to established rivals; to slow the decline of a declining industry so workers and equipment can adjust; to keep strategic industries such as food or defence secure in case conflict or shortage cuts supply; and to counter dumping, where an exporter sells below the cost of production or below its home price to drive rivals out of a market.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The infant-industry chain: a new industry starts small, so its cost per unit tends to sit above established foreign rivals; protection raises the import price or caps the import quantity, so home firms keep sales while they grow; as output grows, the cost per unit tends to fall with scale; where the industry matures, protection may be withdrawn and the industry stands on its own - and where it never matures, consumers keep paying the cost of the shelter.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The anti-dumping chain: an exporter sells below its cost of production to win a foreign market; home producers there lose sales and may close; a tariff or quota raises the dumped import price, so home producers keep their market and their workers keep their jobs; where the protection stays after the dumping stops, consumers keep paying more than the market requires.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The consequences of protection at home: consumers tend to pay higher prices and face less choice, since dearer or scarcer imports no longer hold home prices down; protected home producers keep output and jobs they may otherwise have lost; the government collects the tariff as revenue; and home firms facing less import pressure may put off cutting their own costs.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The consequences for trading partners: the partner exporters sell less, so output and jobs in their export industries tend to fall; their government may retaliate with barriers of its own on the protecting country's exports; and trade between the two countries tends to shrink on both sides.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Protection tends to help the sheltered industry in the short run while spreading its cost across the economy's consumers. It is likely to justify itself where the infant industry genuinely matures or the dumping is real and temporary; it is likely to fail where the shelter removes the pressure to improve, or where partners retaliate and both countries end up trading less.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.
